o1.biggest_strength: Every spoken cell has a real line and the scripts themselves carry the signals — taste-test and swap openings, the '3 pm' line as on-screen text, and the $3 price answered in-scene — so a creator could shoot tomorrow.
o1.biggest_mistake: The hook test is hand-wavy — 'run all nine at the same budget, after about a week' gives no spend per hook, no purchase threshold and no cut rule, so the owner cannot hand it to a media buyer as a decision.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Turn the hook test into a money rule — spend per hook, purchases needed to read, and the cost-per-purchase cut line — so the scripts come with a decision, not just a plan.

o2.biggest_strength: Opens with a why-this-angle table tied to the real view-rate and cost-per-purchase numbers, then backs it with a hook test that sets a $520-per-hook read and a $32 cut line, which is operator-grade.
o2.biggest_mistake: Two spoken cells are left as directions ('their own words on why it works') and it ends with 'To confirm: creator fees and shoot dates,' asking the owner for information they said they could not give.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Fill every spoken cell with an actual line and drop the closing 'To confirm' so the pack is complete on arrival.

reason: Both nail the data and the brand rules, but Output 2 uses the owner's own numbers to justify each angle and turns the hook test into a spend-and-cut rule, while Output 1's test plan is too vague to action. Output 1 is cleaner to shoot and more precise on disclosure, so the edge is small.
